newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-T&N asbestos provisions hit year result.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-T&N asbestos provisions hit year result.

text.p: Auto components maker T&N Plc reported a hefty loss on Wednesday as it booked in its ambitious plan, revealed three months ago, to break free from its past as the Turner & Newall asbestos firm.

The British-based company reported a pretax loss of 388 million pounds ($625 million) for last year, against a 120.1 million pound profit in 1995, after exceptional charges of 515 million pounds for provisions and an insurance policy against future asbestos claims.
It said this gave the group 441 million pounds of provisions and a further 500 million of insurance cover against any future asbestos claims.
The effective dividend payout for the year was held at six pence despite a net loss per share of 75.4 pence due to the provisioning.

T&N's share price slipped three pence to 156-1/2 after it said underlying taxable profits were 95 million pounds last year before exceptional charges. Analysts had forecast the figure at between 78 and 105 million pounds.
"The figures are a bit disappointing compared with the more optimistic expectations," said one trader.
Chairman Sir Colin Hope said the group was looking to restore its operating performance, where margins slipped last year.
Operating profits before the exceptional charges fell to 178 million pounds from 227 million in 1995 on sales down to 1.96 billion pounds from 2.092 billion.
After accounting for disposals, operating profits fell to 173 million pounds from 204 million on sales of 1.89 billion against 1.85 billion a year ago.

Operating margins contracted to 9.1 percent last year from 11 percent in 1995. T&N said this was due to a combination of the cost of job cuts, price pressure from car makers and de-stocking of finished products to boost cash.
But Hope said rationalisation work including some job reductions was now under way to recover its profitability.
"We already have in place new efficiency improvements, new (cost) reductions which ensure those margins will be coming back from now," he told Reuters in an interview.
"We believe that at the peak of the cycle the group should be able to achieve 12 percent plus (margins)...12 percent at the peak and certainly an average 10 percent over the cycle," he said.
T&N said it expected to raise around 70 million pounds from the sale of peripheral businesses this year to help fund the provisions.

When it announced the asbestos provisions in December, it said it intended to create a fund to finance them, to be built up over the next three years from free cash flow, external fund-raising and disposals.

But Hope said on Wednesday all the non-core businesses had been identified and he did not feel rushed to build up the provisioning funds since it was still not certain that the full amount would be needed.

He said there would be big savings in provisions if the U.S. Supreme Court backed the former asbestos industry's appeal to be allowed to continue settling all claims under the Georgine class action procedure.
The Supreme Court is expected to give its ruling on the appeal from the industry by June.

"The way we have done the provisioning at the moment, we have assumed the Georgine appeal fails....If it doesn't, there is about 100 million pounds less possibly needed than we previously thought," he said.
Meanwhile T&N was pursuing its expansion plans with its attempt to take over German firm Kolbenschmidt.
Hope said he expected a Berlin appeals court to give it the formal go-ahead this week to take a 24.99 percent strategic stake in the piston maker.
"I think we are expecting the final ruling literally today or tomorrow," Hope told Reuters.
In a new twist, it was announced later on Wednesday that Rheinmetall planned to buy a separate 24.99 percent stake in Kolbenschmidt from Commerzbank with a view to taking control.
No further details were immediately available but Hope had said earlier in the day he was looking at the possibilities of forming a joint venture with Kolbenschmidt if a takeover proved impossible.
($ = 0.620 British Pounds)
